screens.title: Event-Driven Architectures with Fabric Events
screens.subtitle: Use Fabric events to build reactive, decoupled systems that respond to ledger changes in real time.

narration.text: In distributed ledger systems, waiting for periodic queries to discover state changes creates latency and wasted work. Fabric events give applications an asynchronous channel to be notified as ledger updates happen. In this lesson you will see the different event types Fabric exposes, how a Node. js client subscribes and reacts to events, and how chaincode can publish precise business notifications. We will also examine operational requirements: checkpointing so listeners can recover without losing events, idempotency so repeated deliveries don't corrupt external state, and scaling patterns such as pushing events into a message queue for parallel consumers. A short hands-on activity demonstrates modifying Go chaincode to emit an AssetCreated event and a Node. js listener that logs eventName, payload and transactionId. By the end, you should be able to design a resilient event listener and choose whether to use chaincode events or block events for a given integration. Think about which part of your system must be guaranteed and which can be eventually consistent.

keyIdea.title: Why events matter
keyIdea.text: Fabric events provide asynchronous, targeted notifications that let off-chain services react to ledger changes without costly polling.

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will have four practical competencies. First, you will understand why Fabric events are preferable to polling in many scenarios, and be able to explain when to use block events versus chaincode events. For example, choose chaincode events when you need targeted notifications like an AssetCreated signal. Second, you will learn to subscribe to Fabric event streams using an SDK, including the typical Node. js flow: connect the gateway, get a network and contract, and register a listener. Third, you will implement a resilient listener that uses checkpointing so that after a crash it can resume processing from the last known block. Finally, you will design a production-ready integration that enforces idempotency and optionally pushes events to a message queue for scalable downstream processing. Each objective maps to a verified competency milestone so you can test the listener, the chaincode event emission, and the recovery behavior.

screens.title: Why Fabric events enable reactive systems
screens.subtitle: From polling to asynchronous notifications

narration.text: Fabric events change how off-chain applications stay aware of ledger changes. Polling the ledger requires repeated queries which add load and latency; by contrast, events let your clients subscribe and react only when relevant changes occur, reducing wasted C P U and network overhead. Think of events as a push notification mechanism provided by the Fabric peers: when a block commits or chaincode emits a custom signal, the peer streams that information to subscribers. A concrete example is an order processing system that needs to notify shipping once an order moves to a Confirmed state. If the chaincode emits an OrderConfirmed event, the shipping service receives a concise payload and can start processing immediately. A common misconception is equating events with guaranteed exactly-once semantics; Fabric and many SDKs deliver events at least once or require explicit checks, so your listener must be designed for repeated deliveries. In practice, events improve responsiveness and decoupling, but you must combine them with validation, checkpointing, and idempotent handlers to ensure correctness when retries or replays occur. How will your service react if the same event arrives twice?

keyIdea.title: Reactive instead of polling
keyIdea.text: Use Fabric events to reduce latency and load by pushing notifications for relevant ledger changes rather than continuously querying state.

content.html:
Core Concept Event motivation

Definition

Events are asynchronous notifications emitted by peers or chaincode to inform subscribers about ledger activity.

Why it matters
  • Reduces polling overhead and latency by delivering changes on commit.
  • Decouples producers (chaincode) from consumers (external services).
  • Enables responsive microservices, triggers, and analytics pipelines.
Key Takeaway

Events let consumers react immediately to business outcomes. Combine with safeguards for reliable processing.

Concrete example

A payment chaincode emits PaymentProcessed with payment details. The notification service receives the event and sends an email or SMS without scanning every ledger entry.
Misconception check

Events are not a substitute for validation. Treat event payloads as untrusted until validated by the consuming service, and assume duplicates are possible unless you build stronger guarantees.

Try this

Describe one place in your architecture where a chaincode event would reduce latency. What would you validate before acting on the payload?

screens.title: Block events vs Chaincode events
screens.subtitle: Choose the right event type for your use case

narration.text: Fabric offers multiple event types, and choosing between them affects performance, complexity, and target specificity. Block events are emitted when a new block is committed and contain the full block data including all transactions. They are comprehensive: a consumer can examine every transaction, metadata, and endorsement results. Block events are useful when you need full audit context or must synchronize by block number. Chaincode events, in contrast, are custom signals emitted from within chaincode using SetEvent and are embedded in the transaction that produced them. They are lightweight and targeted: the consumer receives only events relevant to specific business outcomes, such as AssetCreated or OrderConfirmed, with custom payloads. A practical example: for a notification service that only needs to know about completed payments, chaincode events are the better choice because they avoid parsing entire blocks. A common misunderstanding is thinking block events are always safer; while they include everything, they increase processing overhead and require more complex parsing. Consider maintenance cost, payload size, and whether you need transaction-level status when choosing the type. Block events vs Chaincode events means use chaincode events for targeted notifications and block events for full ledger context or auditing needs.. In practical terms, choose the right event type for your use case. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pick by need
keyIdea.text: Use chaincode events for targeted notifications and block events for full ledger context or auditing needs.

content.html:
Comparison Block vs Chaincode
Block events

Emitted on block commit. Contain all transactions and metadata for the block.

  • Use for audit, replay, or full ledger synchronization.
  • Higher parsing and processing cost per event.
  • Can derive transaction status from block contents.
Common use: regulatory reporting or full-state replication.
Chaincode events

Emitted explicitly by chaincode via SetEvent with a name and payload inside the transaction.

  • Targeted messages for business outcomes like AssetCreated.
  • Lower overhead: listener receives fewer irrelevant messages.
  • Payload is defined by chaincode and must be validated by consumers.
Common use: notifying downstream services about specific events.
Decision tip
Choose chaincode events when you need concise, business-focused notifications; choose block events when you need full transaction context.
Performance tip
Avoid parsing entire blocks for simple notifications to reduce CPU and network load.
Security tip
Validate event payloads and use secure channels between SDK and peer (TLS) as recommended.

screens.title: Block events: structure and use cases
screens.subtitle: When to process full blocks

narration.text: Block events provide the entire committed block payload and are generated by peers whenever a block completes consensus and is appended to the ledger. The block includes all transactions, endorsements, read/write sets, and validation codes. Use block events when you need complete visibility of ledger history, such as for auditing, replication, or cross-checking endorsements. For example, a compliance service that reconstructs every ledger change might subscribe to block events to ensure nothing is missed. Processing block events requires parsing all transactions and filtering for relevant chaincode or transaction types, which can be expensive. A typical pitfall is relying on block events for targeted notifications; the consumer ends up doing heavy parsing to find a single business event. If your goal is to trigger a downstream service for a specific business outcome, prefer chaincode events. You should also design block consumers with checkpointing and scaling in mind because replaying or reprocessing blocks can be costly without efficient state management. Block events: structure and use cases means block events give full ledger context and are best for audit or replication, not lightweight notifications.. In practical terms, when to process full blocks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Block event usage
keyIdea.text: Block events give full ledger context and are best for audit or replication, not lightweight notifications.

content.html:
Definition Block events
What a block event contains
  • All transactions in the block and their payloads.
  • Validation codes and read/write sets.
  • Block number and metadata for ordering and auditing.
When to use
  • Ledger replication or rebuilds where full transaction context is required.
  • Forensic audit services that must see all activity in order.
  • Deriving transaction status when SDK helpers are not sufficient.
Performance note
Parsing full blocks is heavier — ensure your listener can keep up or push to a queue for parallel processing.
Design tip
Checkpoint by block number to resume processing exactly where you left off after a failure.
Misconception
Block events are not a low-latency replacement for targeted chaincode events when you only need specific business outcomes.

screens.title: Chaincode events: emit precise business signals
screens.subtitle: Using SetEvent in chaincode

narration.text: Chaincode events are a concise mechanism to publish business-level notifications directly from your chaincode. In Go chaincode you call ctx. GetStub(). SetEvent(eventName, payload) after a state change to embed the event inside the transaction. The eventName is a label like AssetCreated and the payload typically contains a JSON summary of the change. A concrete example: after successfully creating an asset and writing it to world state, call SetEvent with the asset JSON so external listeners can react immediately. Chaincode events are efficient because listeners receive only the named events they care about, so you avoid inspecting each transaction in a block. However, consumers must validate the payload because chaincode defines its structure and could contain unexpected data due to bugs. Also remember that chaincode events travel within transactions and are visible only once the transaction is committed, so listeners should consider transaction finality and potential retries. Emitting events is straightforward, but designing consumers requires care for idempotency and validation. Chaincode events: emit precise business signals means use setevent to signal business outcomes; emit structured payloads and expect consumers to validate and handle duplicates.. In practical terms, using setevent in chaincode. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Chaincode event pattern
keyIdea.text: Use SetEvent to signal business outcomes; emit structured payloads and expect consumers to validate and handle duplicates.

content.html:
Definition Chaincode events
How to emit

Call ctx.GetStub().SetEvent with a name and payload after writing state to the ledger.

Best practices:
  • Emit minimal, structured payloads the listener needs.
  • Keep events meaningful and aligned with business outcomes.
  • Document the payload schema for consumers to validate.
A concrete scenario
After CreateAsset completes and PutState succeeds, emit AssetCreated with the asset JSON. An external listener uses this to update a search index or send notifications.
Safety note

Treat payloads as untrusted until validated. Chaincode bugs can produce malformed data and listeners must verify structure before acting.

Key Takeaway

Chaincode events are the most efficient way to deliver business-level notifications from Fabric to external systems. Validate payloads and design for duplicates.

screens.title: Transaction status and commit events
screens.subtitle: Knowing when a transaction is final

narration.text: Understanding transaction status is essential for correct event-driven behavior. While transactions are proposed and endorsed before ordering, their final validity is determined when a block is committed and validation codes are applied. SDKs often expose utilities to listen for the commit status of a particular transaction ID, which is useful when a client needs confirmation that a specific operation succeeded. Alternatively, you can derive transaction status from block events by parsing the block's validation codes. A concrete example: a payment service submits a transaction and then waits for a commit notification for that transaction ID to confirm the payment was recorded and validated. A common misconception is treating an endorsement as acceptance; endorsements alone do not imply the transaction is committed or valid. For robust flows, combine a commit listener or parse block events to confirm transaction status before triggering irreversible external actions like releasing funds or sending notifications that cannot be retracted. Always design consumers to handle eventual consistency and replays. Transaction status and commit events means confirm transaction commit status before performing irreversible external actions; endorsements are not the final state.. In practical terms, knowing when a transaction is final. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Transaction finality
keyIdea.text: Confirm transaction commit status before performing irreversible external actions; endorsements are not the final state.

content.html:
Core Concept Transaction status

Why commit status matters

Only committed and validated transactions change the ledger state. Consumers should wait for commit confirmation before triggering irreversible side effects.

Patterns:
  • Use SDK commit listeners for transaction-specific confirmation.
  • Or parse block events to derive status for many transactions.
  • Design downstream actions to tolerate retries or rollbacks where possible.

Example

Submit CreateAsset and wait for the SDK's transaction commit notification. Only after commit should the listener update external payment records or notify external systems.

Misconception check

Do not assume endorsements equal finality. Endorsements are part of the transaction life cycle but commitment is the authoritative state change.

screens.title: Subscribing to Fabric events with an SDK
screens.subtitle: Typical steps for a resilient listener

narration.text: Subscribing to Fabric events with an SDK follows a consistent sequence: connect, locate the network, get the contract or event hub, register a listener, and process incoming events. Start by loading the connection profile and wallet, then establish a gateway connection using an enrolled identity. Use the gateway to obtain a network instance for the channel and then get the contract you care about. Register a listener using addContractListener for chaincode events or use the peer's event service for block events. Make sure your listener is non-blocking: heavy work should be forwarded to worker threads or external queues so the event stream stays unblocked. Implement checkpointing by persisting the last processed block number or transaction ID, so on restart you can resume without losing events. Finally, incorporate idempotency checks when applying external side effects to avoid duplicates. In all cases add robust error handling and reconnection logic; network partitions and peer restarts are operational realities. A resilient listener combines these steps into a long-running service with observable checkpoints and backpressure handling. Subscribing to Fabric events with an SDK means connect gateway → get network → get contract → add listener → process events with checkpointing and idempotency.. In practical terms, typical steps for a resilient listener. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Subscribe pattern
keyIdea.text: Connect gateway → get network → get contract → add listener → process events with checkpointing and idempotency.

Process Flow Subscribe
1. Connect
Load connection profile and wallet, then connect the Gateway with the enrolled identity.
2. Get network & contract
Use gateway.getNetwork(channel) and network.getContract(chaincodeName) to scope events.
3. Register listener
Use addContractListener for chaincode events or peer event service for block events.
4. Process non-blocking
Avoid long synchronous work in the listener. Push heavy tasks to workers or queues.
5. Checkpointing
Persist last processed block number or transaction id in durable storage to resume after failure.
6. Idempotency
Design handlers so repeated deliveries do not produce duplicate side effects in external systems.

screens.title: Node.js listener example
screens.subtitle: Read and react to chaincode events with addContractListener

narration.text: Let's walk through a Node. js listener pattern that subscribes to chaincode events and logs details. The sample flow loads the connection profile, opens a file system wallet, and connects a Gateway using an enrolled identity. After getting the network and contract, addContractListener registers a callback invoked for each chaincode event. Inside the callback we access eventName, payload and transactionId, and we should push processing to a worker or queue rather than doing heavy synchronous work in the listener. A concrete scenario: the listener receives AssetCreated with asset JSON; it validates the payload, checks an external database to avoid duplicates, and then updates a search index. A common mistake is using synchronous DB writes inside the listener, which blocks the event stream. Also ensure graceful removal of listeners and gateway. disconnect on shutdown. This sample keeps the process alive to demonstrate behavior, but production services should implement reconnection, checkpointing, and persistent logging for observability. How would you design the validation step for your payloads? Node.js listener example means use addcontractlistener, validate payloads, and avoid blocking the callback; forward heavy work to durable workers or queues.. In practical terms, read and react to chaincode events with addcontractlistener. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Listener pattern
keyIdea.text: Use addContractListener, validate payloads, and avoid blocking the callback; forward heavy work to durable workers or queues.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough Node.js listener
Example code (excerpt)
// register listener
const listener = await contract.addContractListener('myEventListener', (event) => {
  console.log('Chaincode Event:', event.eventName);
  console.log('Payload:', event.payload ? event.payload.toString('utf8') : '');
  console.log('Transaction ID:', event.transactionId);
  // Validate payload, then enqueue processing for workers
});
Note: This excerpt omits connection and wallet setup for brevity.
Processing checklist
  • Validate structure and types of the payload before acting.
  • Check external DB for existing records to ensure idempotency.
  • Push heavy work to an asynchronous worker or message queue.
  • Persist a checkpoint after successful processing to allow resume.
Operational tip: Log transactionId and blockNumber for traceability.

narration.text: Emitting a chaincode event in Go is straightforward and powerful when used correctly. After you create and persist an asset in CreateAsset using PutState, call ctx. GetStub(). SetEvent with a descriptive event name like AssetCreated and include the JSON payload. The payload should be minimal and machine-friendly so listeners can parse it easily. A concrete walkthrough: marshal your asset to JSON, write it to world state, check the error, then call SetEvent and handle any failure to ensure the transaction either succeeds with the event or fails cleanly. Remember that the event is part of the transaction and only visible after commit. Listeners will receive the event embedded in the committed transaction. A common mistake is emitting events before the state write succeeds or embedding large payloads that bloat the transaction. Keep events compact and always validate payload schema in the consumer. This approach yields precise notifications while keeping chaincode logic clear and auditable. Emitting events from Go chaincode means call setevent after putstate succeeds; emit compact json payloads and handle errors to keep chaincode and events consistent.. In practical terms, setevent in createasset. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: SetEvent pattern
keyIdea.text: Call SetEvent after PutState succeeds; emit compact JSON payloads and handle errors to keep chaincode and events consistent.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough Go chaincode
Modified CreateAsset (excerpt)
assetJSON, err := json.Marshal(asset)
if err != nil { return err }
err = ctx.GetStub().PutState(asset.ID, assetJSON)
if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("failed to put to world state: %v", err) }
err = ctx.GetStub().SetEvent("AssetCreated", assetJSON)
if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("failed to set event: %w", err) }
Keep payloads compact and validate consumer-side.
Design notes
  • Emit events only after state write succeeds to avoid inconsistencies.
  • Limit payload size; include identifiers listeners can use to fetch full state if needed.
  • Document event names and payload schemas for consumers.
Testing tip: invoke CreateAsset and confirm the listener prints eventName and payload.

narration.text: Checkpointing records the last successfully processed point in an event stream so a listener can resume without losing or reprocessing too many events. In a Fabric context you might persist the last processed block number or the last transaction ID to durable storage. On restart, the listener reads the checkpoint and asks the SDK or event hub to stream events from that point. A robust checkpoint strategy includes atomic commits: mark an event as processed only after all side effects are durably stored and the checkpoint itself is persisted. Consider storing both the checkpoint and a processing offset in the same transactional store to avoid inconsistencies. A common pitfall is persisting the checkpoint before downstream work completes; that leads to data loss if the service crashes after checkpointing but before applying changes. Another option is to push raw events to a message queue first and let consumers process messages with their own checkpoints; this introduces buffer durability at the cost of extra components. In all cases test recovery by simulating crashes and verifying no events are missed or duplicated beyond acceptable bounds.

keyIdea.title: Checkpoint reliably
keyIdea.text: Persist the last processed block or transaction only after downstream work is durably stored, and test restart scenarios to avoid missed events.

content.html:
Core Concept Checkpointing
Checkpoint patterns
  • Store last processed block number in a durable database after successful processing.
  • Use transaction IDs for finer-grained resume points when processing per-transaction.
  • Push events to a queue first if you want durable buffering outside the listener process.
Pitfall to avoid: Writing the checkpoint before downstream updates finish. Instead, make checkpointing the last step of an atomic processing sequence.
Try this

Simulate a crash after processing but before checkpointing. Verify your recovery logic reprocesses the necessary events without causing duplicates in the external system.

narration.text: Idempotency ensures that processing the same event multiple times yields the same result as processing it once. This property is central to reliable Fabric event consumers because network partitions and retries can cause at-least-once delivery. Implement idempotency by using unique event identifiers—transactionId or a composite key—and checking whether the external action has already been applied before making changes. For example, when an AssetCreated event arrives, the consumer should check if the asset already exists in its database; if it does, skip creation or update safely. Error handling must be explicit: transient errors should trigger retries with exponential backoff, while permanent validation failures must be logged and quarantined for manual inspection. Also avoid blocking listeners: if a transient failure occurs, move the event to a retry queue and continue processing new events. A common mistake is assuming the event stream is ordered and unique; always plan for duplicates and reordering where applicable. Combining idempotency with checkpointing yields predictable recovery behavior and consistent external state. Idempotency and error handling means use transaction ids and existence checks to ensure repeated event deliveries do not create duplicate side effects; separate retry logic from main processing.. In practical terms, design consumers that tolerate retries. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Idempotent design
keyIdea.text: Use transaction IDs and existence checks to ensure repeated event deliveries do not create duplicate side effects; separate retry logic from main processing.

content.html:
Core Concept Idempotency
How to be idempotent
  • Use transactionId as a unique key and record processed IDs.
  • Check external system state before creating or updating records.
  • Store processing results and checkpoint only after durable write.
Error handling
  • Retry transient failures asynchronously with backoff.
  • Quarantine and alert on validation failures for manual review.
  • Avoid blocking the listener loop; move retries to a worker queue.

screens.title: Scaling and integrating with message queues
screens.subtitle: Buffering, parallel consumers, and throughput

narration.text: For high-volume event streams, push Fabric events into a durable message queue such as Kafka or RabbitMQ before processing. The event listener acts as a producer that forwards events to the queue, decoupling ingestion from processing and enabling multiple consumers to scale horizontally. This architecture improves resilience because the queue buffers bursts and provides persistence if consumers fall behind. A concrete deployment: the listener receives chaincode events, validates minimal payloads, and publishes messages to a topic partitioned by asset ID so related updates are processed in order. Consumers read from the queue, perform idempotent updates against external systems, and commit their own checkpoints or offsets. Consider trade-offs: adding a queue increases component complexity and operational overhead but greatly improves throughput and fault tolerance. Always ensure TLS and authentication between the listener and queue, and include observability so you can track backpressure and consumer lag. Which partitioning strategy would keep related updates ordered in your system? Scaling and integrating with message queues means use a durable message queue to buffer events, enable parallel consumers, and absorb bursts while preserving processing guarantees.. In practical terms, buffering, parallel consumers, and throughput. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Queue integration
keyIdea.text: Use a durable message queue to buffer events, enable parallel consumers, and absorb bursts while preserving processing guarantees.

content.html:
Architecture Scaling
Pattern
  1. Listener subscribes to Fabric and validates events.
  2. Listener publishes events to a durable queue or topic.
  3. Multiple consumers process messages in parallel with idempotency checks.
Trade-offs
  • Pros: buffering, parallelism, and better resilience to spikes.
  • Cons: added operational components and potential ordering complexity.
  • Ensure secure transport and monitor consumer lag closely.
Key Takeaway

Introduce a queue between Fabric and consumers to scale processing and decouple ingestion from downstream work, but account for ordering and operational cost.

narration.text: These three core ideas will guide your event-driven designs with Fabric. First, Fabric Events are asynchronous notifications from peers and chaincode that let you build reactive services without polling. Second, checkpointing and idempotency are operational musts: persist progress and make handlers safe to replay so the system tolerates crashes and retries. Third, choose the right event type and integration pattern: chaincode events are ideal for targeted business notifications while block events provide full ledger context; use durable queues to scale high-throughput workloads. Keep event payloads compact, validate them before acting, and avoid blocking listeners. With these practices you'll build decoupled, resilient integrations that surface ledger changes to external systems reliably. Key Concepts means events, checkpointing, and idempotency form the foundation of reliable fabric integrations; choose event types and architectures based on your notification, audit, and scaling needs.. In practical terms, what to remember. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Core takeaways
keyIdea.text: Events, checkpointing, and idempotency form the foundation of reliable Fabric integrations; choose event types and architectures based on your notification, audit, and scaling needs.

Summary Key Concepts
Fabric Events
Asynchronous notifications for ledger updates and business outcomes.
Checkpointing
Persist last-processed block or txn so listeners can resume reliably.
Idempotency
Ensure repeated processing does not cause duplicate or inconsistent external state.
Takeaway

Use chaincode events for targeted notifications, block events for full context, and design listeners with checkpointing, validation, and idempotency to ensure correctness.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three final reminders for reliable event-driven design

narration.text: Keep these final reminders in mind when building Fabric-driven systems. First, prefer chaincode events when you want targeted, efficient notifications, and use block events only when you need full transaction context. Second, always persist checkpoints only after downstream work is durable, and test recovery paths by simulating restarts. Third, design all event handlers to be idempotent and validate event payloads before acting. Together these practices preserve correctness and enable scalable integrations. As you implement your listener and modify chaincode, run the hands-on activity: emit AssetCreated from your Go chaincode, run the Node. js listener, trigger CreateAsset, and observe the event flow. That exercise ties the concepts together and demonstrates how events, checkpoints, and idempotency produce reliable, reactive systems. Key Concepts — Quick Reference means prefer targeted chaincode events, checkpoint after durable writes, and make handlers idempotent to build reliable integrations.. In practical terms, three final reminders for reliable event-driven design. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
What to Remember Quick reference
Choose event type
Chaincode events for business signals; block events for full ledger context.
Checkpoint safely
Only advance checkpoints after durable downstream writes to avoid data loss.
Design idempotent consumers
Use transactionId checks and existence queries to prevent duplicates.
Next step

Try the hands-on activity: emit AssetCreated in your chaincode, run the Node.js listener, and verify event logging and recovery behavior.

ai_generation_note: Create a 10-minute live coding video. Start with a basic `asset-transfer` chaincode and modify its `CreateAsset` function to emit a `AssetCreated` chaincode event with the asset's JSON payload. Then, demonstrate a Node.js client application subscribing to this event. Show the terminal output of the listener reacting in real-time as new assets are created via a separate `peer chaincode invoke` command. Include a visual overlay explaining the `SetEvent` function in chaincode and the `addContractListener` in the SDK. Discuss the importance of checkpointing and idempotency. End with a reflection prompt on how to design an event-driven microservice that integrates with Fabric.
